title: Sorting materials: putting things into groups by asking a question

summary.text: A steel spoon sinks in a bucket of water, but a steel katori floats. Both are steel. Sorting means putting things into groups by asking one question about each thing, such as 'Is it metal?' Your child sorts kitchen things by material, then sorts the same things again with a water test. They find that the metal group splits in two, and they find out why.
summary.art: A girl kneeling beside a bucket of water. A steel katori floats on top, and a steel spoon, a key and a coin lie at the bottom. Beside the bucket are two small piles of kitchen things.

intro.hook: Here are six things: a steel spoon, a pencil, a comb, a key, a bottle cap and a wooden spoon. Can you put them into two groups? What question did you ask to make your groups?
intro.text: People sort things every day. A grandmother in Kochi puts the steel vessels on one shelf and the glass jars on another. In Mumbai, the dabbawalas sort thousands of tiffin boxes by the marks on the lids. To sort, you ask one question about each thing, like 'Is it metal?' If the answer is yes, the thing goes in one group. If the answer is no, it goes in the other group.
intro.art: Three small pictures side by side: a grandmother putting steel vessels on a shelf, a dabbawala in a white cap sorting tiffin boxes with painted marks, and a bangle seller with rows of red and green bangles.

outcomes: By the end I can sort things into two groups by asking one question, like 'Is it metal?'
By the end I can say what a thing is made of, and put it in the right material group.
By the end I can find a tricky thing that does not fit one group, and use a test to decide where it goes.
By the end I can say that things made of one material can act differently: a steel spoon sinks, but a steel katori floats.
By the end I can guess what will happen, say why, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, paper and cloth are materials.
terms.example: A spoon can be made of the material steel, or wood, or plastic.
terms.art: Three spoons in a row: a shiny steel spoon, a brown wooden spoon and a red plastic spoon.

terms.meaning: To sort is to put things that are alike together, and things that are different apart.
terms.example: After washing up, a grandmother sorts the spoons into one tumbler and the forks into another.
terms.art: A grandmother's hands putting spoons into one steel tumbler and forks into another.

terms.meaning: A group is a set of things that are alike in one way.
terms.example: A key, a coin and a steel spoon make a group of metal things.
terms.art: A key, a coin and a steel spoon lying together inside a circle of string.

terms.meaning: A test is something you do to find out an answer, instead of only guessing.
terms.example: Tap a tumbler with a spoon. If it rings with a 'ting', it is probably metal.
terms.art: A girl tapping a steel tumbler with a spoon, with small lines around the tumbler to show it ringing.

terms.meaning: A thing floats when it stays up on top of the water.
terms.example: A pencil dropped in a bucket of water floats.
terms.art: A yellow pencil floating on the water in a blue bucket.

terms.meaning: A thing sinks when it goes down to the bottom of the water.
terms.example: A one-rupee coin dropped in a bucket of water sinks.
terms.art: A coin lying at the bottom of a bucket of water, with a few bubbles above it.

explanations.concept: Sorting means putting alike things together
explanations.definition: To sort is to put things into groups, so that the things in each group are alike in one way.
explanations.description: When you sort, you look at each thing and decide which group it belongs in. You can sort spoons, toys, clothes, leaves or anything else. Sorting helps us find things quickly. It also helps us notice how things are alike and how they are different.
examples: Socks go in one drawer and shirts in another, so you can find them fast.
A kabadiwala keeps newspaper, bottles and tins in separate heaps, because each one is sold to a different buyer.
A bangle seller in Hyderabad sorts bangles by colour, so each customer can find the colour she wants.
explanations.context: This card says what sorting is. You did it in the Yes-or-No Sort.
explanations.art: A child's room with socks in one open drawer and shirts in another, and a small girl holding up one sock.

explanations.definition: To sort, you ask the same question about every thing. If the answer is yes, the thing goes in one group. If the answer is no, it goes in the other group.
explanations.description: The question 'Is it metal?' makes two groups: metal things and things that are not metal. The question 'Is it made of wood?' makes two different groups. You can sort the same heap with many questions. Each question gives new groups. A good sorting question has a clear answer for each thing.
examples: 'Is it metal?' puts a key and a coin together, and a pencil and a comb in the other group.
'Is it made of plastic?' puts a comb and a bottle cap together.
'Is it red?' is a sorting question too, but it tells you nothing about the material.
explanations.context: This card is about the question you ask when you sort.
explanations.art: Two circles of dupatta on the floor, one labelled YES and one labelled NO, with a key and a coin in the YES circle and a pencil and a comb in the NO circle.

explanations.concept: A test settles a tricky thing
explanations.definition: When you are not sure which group a thing belongs in, you can do a test to find out.
explanations.description: Looking is not always enough. A clear bottle might be glass or plastic. So you test: tap it and listen, feel if it is cold, lift it and feel how heavy it is. A knife has a steel blade and a plastic handle, so it can go in both groups.
examples: Tap a clear bottle with a spoon. Glass goes ting, and plastic goes tock.
A steel spoon feels cold in your hand. A plastic spoon of the same size feels warmer.
A steel tiffin is heavier than a plastic tiffin of the same size.
explanations.context: This card is about things that are hard to sort, and how to decide where they go.
explanations.art: A girl tapping a clear bottle with a spoon and listening carefully, with a second clear bottle beside it.

explanations.concept: Why the steel katori floats and the steel spoon sinks
explanations.definition: Water pushes up on everything you put in it. A thing floats when that push is strong enough to hold it up.
explanations.description: A steel spoon is small and solid, so the water cannot hold it up and it sinks. A steel katori is wide and hollow, with air inside. Steel and air together are light for the space they take up, so the water holds the katori up. Fill it with water, and the air is pushed out, so it sinks. Big steel ships float in the same way.
examples: A one-rupee coin sinks, but a big wooden log floats. So heavy things do not always sink.
A steel ship at the port in Kochi weighs more than many elephants together, yet it floats.
A rubber ball floats on water, but a pebble of the same size sinks.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Sink or Float Sort, where the steel spoon and the steel katori did different things.
explanations.art: Side by side: a steel spoon at the bottom of a bucket, and a steel katori floating with small arrows under it pointing up to show the water pushing.

agreed.text: Things can be sorted into groups by what they are made of.
agreed.evidence: Every thing around us is made of one or more materials that can be named, so each thing can be put in a material group.

agreed.text: The same heap can be sorted in many ways, by asking different questions.
agreed.evidence: Sort a heap by 'Is it metal?' and then by 'Does it float?', and you get different groups from the same things.

agreed.text: Whether a thing floats depends on its material and its shape.
agreed.evidence: A steel spoon sinks and a steel katori floats. Steel ships float too, because their shape holds a lot of air.

challenging.claim: Heavy things sink and light things float.
challenging.who: Many children, and many grown-ups too
challenging.for: A heavy stone sinks, and a light leaf floats.
challenging.against: A small, light key sinks. A big, heavy log floats, and a huge steel ship floats. So weight alone does not tell you whether a thing floats.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess about floating.

challenging.who: Most of us, because spoons, keys and coins sink
challenging.for: A solid lump of metal, like a coin or a key, does sink.
challenging.against: In the Sink or Float Sort, the steel katori floated. Ships made of steel float on the sea every day.
challenging.context: This card is about metal and floating.

challenging.who: Most of us, because plastic things look and feel alike
challenging.for: Plastic things are often light and smooth, and they come in every colour.
challenging.against: There are many kinds of plastic. Some float in water and some sink.
challenging.context: This card is about the plastic group, and why it can split.

big_questions.q: The katori is steel, with air inside it. Is it a steel thing or an air thing?
big_questions.hint: Float the katori empty, with air inside it. Then fill it with water. What changed?

big_questions.q: If a thing fits in two groups, which one is the right group?
big_questions.hint: Think of a knife with a steel blade and a plastic handle.

big_questions.q: Who makes the groups: the things, or the person sorting them?
big_questions.hint: Could you sort your toys in a way nobody else has ever tried?

big_questions.q: Do other animals sort things too?
big_questions.hint: Watch a crow pick through a heap of food. Does she take everything, or choose some things?

roots.context: We have sorted things by what they are made of, and then by whether they float. Now we ask what the floating katori tells us about things, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Sink or Float Sort, the steel spoon sank, but the steel katori floated. When you filled the katori with water, it sank too. The air inside its hollow shape had held it up. So whether a thing floats depends on its material and on the air its shape holds.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things by material and expect everything in one group to act the same: metal sinks, wood floats. But a thing is its material and its shape together, and the shape can hold air.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sink or Float Sort, the spoon, the coin and the key sank, while the katori floated. Once the katori was filled with water, it went to the bottom like the spoon.

three.who_am_i: You are made of many materials: bone, muscle, skin and blood. Your lungs hold air too. With your lungs full of air, you float more easily in water, like the katori.
three.what_is_life: Living beings sort things all the time. A crow picks out the food she wants from a heap. Your tongue sorts sweet from bitter.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has many materials, and each one can be made into many shapes. A material and its shape together decide what a thing can do.

roots.thread: A heap of spoons, keys, combs and pencils can be sorted into a few materials: metal, wood and plastic. But the same steel can be a spoon that sinks or a katori that floats, because the shape holds air. Everything is conscious: the steel, the water, the air, and the child who sorts them.

teachings.teaching: We shape clay into a pot. But it is the empty space inside that makes the pot useful.
teachings.link: The katori's empty space, full of air, is what kept it on top of the water. When water filled that space, it sank.

teachings.source: The Vaisheshika Sutra of the sage Kanada
teachings.teaching: Kanada sorted everything in the world into a few kinds. He taught that earth, water, fire and air are made of tiny parts, far too small to see. He called these tiny parts paramanu.
teachings.link: Like you, Kanada sorted things by asking what they are made of. Today scientists call the tiny parts of every material atoms.

science.text: Water pushes up on anything put in it. More than 2,200 years ago, Archimedes of Syracuse wrote about this push in his book On Floating Bodies.
Scientists have made a solid called aerogel that is almost all air. It is among the lightest solids ever made.

other_view.view: Many scientists say that steel, water and air are only materials, and that only living beings with brains are aware.

practice.title: Fill up like a katori
practice.say: Sit up tall and put your hand on your tummy. Breathe in slowly through your nose. Feel your body fill with air, like the katori. Now breathe out slowly. Feel the air go. Do it three times.
practice.kid: Put your hand on your tummy. Breathe in slowly. Fill up with air, like the katori. Breathe out slowly. Do it three times.

ask: The katori was steel and air together. Which group should it go in?
If you sort the same things a new way, do the things change, or only the groups?
You are full of air when you breathe in. What group would you put yourself in?
roots.art: A girl sitting cross-legged with her hand on her tummy, breathing in, and beside her a steel katori floating on a bucket of water.

how_we_found_out.story: Long ago, thinkers in Greece and in India sorted all the materials of the world into a few big kinds. In India, the five elements, the pancha bhuta, were earth, water, fire, air and space. For more than 2,000 years, most people thought water was a basic material that could not be made from anything else. Then, in the 1780s, an English scientist named Henry Cavendish burned a gas, and drops of water appeared. In France, Antoine Lavoisier tested this carefully. He showed that water is made of two gases joined together, and he named one of them hydrogen, which means 'water-maker'. His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, worked beside him. She kept notes and drew the experiments, and her drawings were printed in his book of 1789. That book sorted materials into 33 basic substances, called elements. Some were wrong: it listed light and heat. Today scientists know 118 elements.
how_we_found_out.who: Henry Cavendish, an English scientist; Antoine Lavoisier, a French scientist; and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, who worked with him and drew the pictures of their experiments
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Water is a basic material that cannot be made from anything else. Cavendish and Lavoisier showed that water is made of two gases joined together.

story.title: The Ladle That Had No Shelf
story.note: Kochi is a city in Kerala. Ammamma means grandmother in Malayalam. A chiratta ladle is a spoon made from half a coconut shell with a wooden handle. Lakshmi, Kannan and Ammamma are made up.
text: Lakshmi was six. She lived in a flat on the fourth floor in Kochi, with her little brother Kannan and their grandmother, Ammamma.
One Sunday, a carpenter came and fixed a new rack in the kitchen. It had four empty shelves.
'Now we can put everything in its place,' said Ammamma. 'Who will help me sort?'
'Me!' said Lakshmi. 'Me too!' said Kannan, who was four.
Ammamma spread a mat on the floor. She took everything out of the old cupboard and put it on the mat. There were tumblers and plates, jars and boxes, spoons and ladles. It was a big, jumbled heap.
'How shall we sort it?' asked Ammamma.
Lakshmi looked at the heap. 'By what it is made of,' she said. 'One shelf for steel, one for glass, one for plastic, and one for wood.'
'Good,' said Ammamma. 'For each thing, ask: what is it made of?'
Kannan picked up a tumbler. It was cold and shiny. He tapped it with a spoon. Ting!
'Steel!' he said, and put it on the steel shelf.
Lakshmi picked up a jar. She could see right through it. She tapped it. It went ting too, but a softer ting.
'Is it glass or plastic?' she asked.
'Lift it,' said Ammamma. Lakshmi lifted it. It was heavy for its size.
'Glass,' said Lakshmi. 'Plastic would be lighter.' She put it gently on the glass shelf.
The red lunch box was light and went tock. Plastic. The rolling pin had thin brown lines on it. Wood. One by one, the heap got smaller, and the shelves filled up.
Then Kannan held up the last thing. It was a ladle. Its handle was a stick of wood, and its bowl was round and brown and a little hairy on the outside.
'Wood,' said Kannan, and he reached for the wood shelf.
'Wait,' said Lakshmi. She took the ladle and looked at the bowl. 'This part has no lines. And it has hairs on the back. Wood does not have hairs.'
Ammamma smiled. 'That is my chiratta ladle. The bowl is half a coconut shell. My mother made ladles like that, and her mother too.'
'So it is not wood,' said Lakshmi. 'And it is not steel or glass or plastic. It has no shelf!'
Kannan frowned. 'Then where does it go?'
They all looked at the ladle.
'A coconut shell comes from a coconut palm,' said Lakshmi slowly. 'And wood comes from a tree. Both come from plants.'
'That is true,' said Ammamma. 'The coconut shell is not wood. But it is hard like wood, and it comes from a plant, like wood does.'
'Then let's change the shelf,' said Lakshmi. 'Not the wood shelf. The plant shelf.'
Ammamma laughed. 'A new group for a new thing. That is how sorting works.'
So the chiratta ladle went on the bottom shelf, next to the rolling pin and the wooden spoon. Lakshmi drew a little palm tree on a piece of paper and stuck the paper on the edge of the shelf.
Then Kannan pulled the cotton kitchen towel off the rail. 'Cotton grows on a plant,' he said. 'Does this go on the plant shelf too?'
Lakshmi thought about it. 'It does come from a plant,' she said. 'But it is cloth. It needs to hang up and dry.'
'So it could go in two groups,' said Ammamma. 'The plant group and the cloth group. You choose where it is most useful.'
Kannan hung the towel back on the rail.
That night, Lakshmi lay in bed and looked around her room. Her toys were in a heap in the corner. Steel car. Plastic doll. Wooden blocks. Cloth rabbit.
'Tomorrow,' she thought, 'I will sort them. But maybe not by material. Maybe by which ones Kannan is allowed to play with.'
She smiled and fell asleep.
story.epiphany: To sort, ask one question about every thing. When a thing does not fit any group, you can make a new group, and some things fit in two groups.
ask: Why did Kannan think the chiratta ladle was wood? Why did Lakshmi think it was not?
Lakshmi made a new group for the ladle. What was the new group?
How else could Lakshmi sort her toys?
art: A grandmother and two children on a kitchen floor around a heap of tumblers, jars, boxes and ladles, with a new four-shelf rack behind them.
A boy tapping a steel tumbler with a spoon, and a girl lifting a glass jar to feel how heavy it is.
A girl holding a coconut-shell ladle and looking at its hairy brown back, while her grandmother smiles.

experiments.title: The Sink or Float Sort: does the metal group stay together?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sort eight kitchen things by material. Then you guess which ones will float in a bucket of water, and test each one. You find out whether all the things in one material group do the same thing.
experiments.question: If we sort things by material, do all the things in one group float or sink together?
experiments.predict: Look at the metal group and the wood group. Which things will float, and which will sink? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every thing goes into the same bucket of water, one at a time. Each one is put in gently, right way up, and we watch it for the same time: a count of five.

materials.item: a bucket or a big vessel, half full of water
a steel spoon
a light steel katori or small bowl, wide and thin (a thick, heavy one may sink)
a one-rupee coin
a key
a wooden spoon, or an ice-cream stick
a pencil
a plastic bottle cap
a plastic comb
a tumbler of water, to fill the katori at the end
an old towel for the floor, and paper and crayons for the results

schedule.what: Sort eight things by material, guess which will float, test each one in a bucket of water, then fill the katori and test it again.

experiments.record: Fold a paper in half. Write or draw FLOAT at the top of one side and SINK at the top of the other. Draw each thing on the side where it ended up. Colour all the metal things grey.

setup.art: Eight things on a towel in three piles: a steel spoon, a katori, a coin and a key in one; a wooden spoon and a pencil in another; a bottle cap and a comb in a third.
setup.caption: 1. Sort the eight things into metal, wood and plastic.

setup.art: A girl gently putting a steel katori, right way up, onto the water in a blue bucket, while a grown-up watches.
setup.caption: 2. Put each thing in the water gently. Does it float or sink?

setup.art: A bucket seen from the side: a katori, a pencil, a wooden spoon and a bottle cap floating on top, and a spoon, a coin, a key and a comb at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Make a float group and a sink group.

setup.art: A girl pouring water from a tumbler into the floating katori, and the katori tipping down into the water.
setup.caption: 4. Fill the katori with water. What happens now?

flow.do: 1. Spread the towel on the floor and put the bucket on it. 2. Put the eight things on the towel. 3. Your child sorts them into material groups.
flow.say: Here are eight things. Let's sort them by what they are made of. Which ones are metal? Which are wood? Which are plastic?
flow.kid: Sort the eight things. Make a metal group, a wood group and a plastic group.

ask.q: How do you know the katori is metal?
good: It rings when I tap it.
It is steel, like the spoon.

flow.parent: Expect a metal group of four, a wood group of two and a plastic group of two. If your child is not sure, tap each thing with a spoon and listen.

flow.do: 1. Point to the metal group, then the wood group, then the plastic group. 2. For each thing, your child says float or sink, and why. 3. Write or draw each guess. A grown-up writes the words.
flow.say: Now guess. Will this one float or sink when we put it in the water? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at each thing. Will it float or sink? Say why.

good: Metal is heavy, so it will sink.
The katori looks like a boat.

flow.parent: Wait for a reason with every guess. Many children say 'all metal sinks'. Don't correct this. The test in the water will show them.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts one thing at a time gently into the water. 2. Put the katori in right way up, so no water spills in. 3. Count to five together for each one. 4. Leave each thing where it lands.
flow.say: Put it in gently. One, two, three, four, five. Did it float or sink? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Put one thing in the water gently. Count to five. Float or sink?

good: It stayed on top like a boat.

flow.parent: The spoon, the coin and the key sink at once. The katori floats if you lower it gently, right way up. The wooden spoon, the pencil and the bottle cap float. Many plastic combs sink, but some float, because there are many kinds of plastic. Either result is fine. If your katori sinks even when placed gently, use a wider, thinner steel bowl instead.

flow.do: 1. Take the floaters out and make one pile. 2. Take the sinkers out and make another pile. 3. Ask your child to look at the metal things.
flow.say: Look at the float pile and the sink pile. Where did the metal things go? Did they all stay together?
flow.kid: Look at your two piles. Where are the metal things?

ask.q: What happened to the metal group?
good: The katori floated, but the spoon sank.
Some metal floats and some sinks.

flow.parent: This is the surprise of the test. The metal group did not stay together. Let your child say it in their own words.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for an idea. 2. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: The spoon and the katori are both steel. So why did the katori float? What is different about it?
flow.kid: The spoon and the katori are both steel. Why did only the katori float?

good: The katori is big and round.
It is shaped like a boat.

flow.do: 1. Lower the katori onto the water again, right way up. 2. Your child pours water into the katori from the tumbler until it is full.
flow.say: Let's test your idea. The katori is floating. Now pour water into it, slowly. Watch what happens.
flow.kid: Pour water into the floating katori. Watch it.

good: It filled up and went down.
It went to the bottom like the spoon.

flow.parent: As the katori fills, it sinks lower, and then it tips and goes down. The air inside it has been pushed out by the water.

flow.do: 1. Say together what you found. 2. Your child draws the results. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: The katori floated when it was full of air. It sank when it was full of water. So what kept it up?
flow.kid: What kept the katori up? Draw your float side and your sink side.

good: The water pushed it up, because it had air.

check.q: The steel spoon sank, but the steel katori floated. Why?
options: The katori's shape held air inside it
The katori was made of lighter steel
The water was colder for the katori
check.why: Both are steel. The katori's wide, hollow shape held air, so steel and air together were light enough for the water to hold up. When water filled it, the air was gone and it sank.

activities.title: The Yes-or-No Sort: is it metal?
activities.context: In this activity you make two circles on the floor, a yes circle and a no circle. You ask one question about each thing, 'Is it metal?', and put it in the right circle. Then you make up a question of your own.

materials.item: two dupattas, two towels or two pieces of string, to make two circles on the floor
ten safe things from the kitchen, such as a steel spoon, a key, a coin, a steel tumbler, a wooden spoon, a pencil, a plastic comb, a plastic bottle cap, a cotton hanky and a paper bag
a blunt table knife with a steel blade and a plastic handle, held by the grown-up only

activities.safety: Only the grown-up holds the knife, and only by the handle.

schedule.what: Sort ten things with the question 'Is it metal?', decide about the knife, then sort again with your own question.

activities.record: Draw the two circles on paper. Draw the things in the yes circle and the no circle. Write the question at the top.

setup.art: Two circles made of dupattas on a floor, one with a tick card and one with a cross card, and ten kitchen things in a heap beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Make a yes circle and a no circle.

setup.art: A small girl holding a key over the yes circle, with a steel spoon and a coin already inside it and a pencil and a comb in the no circle.
setup.caption: 2. Ask 'Is it metal?' Put each thing in a circle.

flow.do: 1. Lay out two circles on the floor. 2. Put a tick drawn on paper in one and a cross in the other. 3. Put the ten things in a heap.
flow.say: This circle is for yes, and this one is for no. For each thing, we ask one question: is it metal?
flow.kid: Here are two circles. Tick means yes. Cross means no. Ask: is it metal?

flow.do: 1. Your child picks up each thing and asks 'Is it metal?' 2. They put it in the yes circle or the no circle. 3. Ask how they know.
flow.say: Is the key metal? How do you know? Put it in the yes circle or the no circle.
flow.kid: Pick a thing. Is it metal? Put it in a circle. Say how you know.

ask.q: How do you know it is metal?
good: It goes ting when I tap it.

flow.parent: If your child is not sure, try three tests: tap it with a spoon, hold it to feel if it is cold, and lift it to feel the weight.

flow.do: Hold up the knife by its handle. Ask where it should go.
flow.say: Look at this knife. The blade is steel and the handle is plastic. Which circle does it go in?
flow.kid: Look at the knife. Part of it is metal. Part is plastic. Where does it go?

good: Half in yes and half in no.

flow.parent: Lay the knife across the edge of both circles, so the blade is in yes and the handle is in no. Some things are made of two materials.

flow.do: 1. Mix all the things up again. 2. Your child makes up a new question. 3. Sort again with that question.
flow.say: Now you choose a new question. It could be 'Is it soft?' or 'Is it made of plastic?' Let's sort again.
flow.kid: Make up a new question. Sort all the things again.

ask.q: What new groups did your question make?
good: Soft things: the hanky and the paper bag.
Plastic things: the comb and the cap.

check.q: You ask 'Is it metal?' about a coin, a pencil and a key. Which one goes in the no circle?
check.why: A coin and a key are metal, so they go in the yes circle. A pencil is mostly wood, so it goes in the no circle.

activities.title: Odd One Out Trays
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up puts four things on a plate. Three are made of the same material and one is different. You find the odd one out and say why. Then you make a plate for the grown-up.

materials.item: two steel plates
small things made of metal, wood, plastic, cloth and paper, about sixteen in all
a steel tumbler and an empty chips packet, for the last plate

schedule.what: Find the odd one out on three plates, then make a plate for the grown-up to solve.

activities.record: Draw your best odd-one-out plate. Put a ring around the odd one.

setup.art: A steel plate with a steel spoon, a key, a coin and a pencil on it.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the four things. Which one is different?

setup.art: A girl putting four things on a plate while a grown-up covers their eyes.
setup.caption: 2. Now make a plate for the grown-up.

flow.do: 1. Put a steel spoon, a key, a coin and a pencil on a plate. 2. Ask which one is the odd one out. 3. Do two more plates, for example three plastic things and a wooden spoon, then three cloth things and a paper bag.
flow.say: Three of these are made of the same material. One is different. Which one is the odd one out? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the four things. Which one is different? Why?

ask.q: Why is the pencil the odd one out?
good: It is wood, and the others are metal.

flow.parent: Your child may choose a different odd one out for a different reason, such as 'the spoon is the longest'. Say that is a good sort too, then ask which one is the odd one out by material.

flow.do: 1. Cover your eyes. 2. Your child chooses four things and puts them on the other plate. 3. Open your eyes and guess.
flow.say: Now you make a plate for me. Put three things of one material and one different thing on it. I will close my eyes.
flow.kid: Make a plate for the grown-up. Three the same, one different.
flow.parent: Guess out loud and give your reason. Get one wrong on purpose, and let your child explain why.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a tricky plate: a steel spoon, a steel tumbler, a key and a shiny chips packet. Which one is the odd one out?
flow.kid: Which is the odd one out: spoon, tumbler, key or chips packet?

check.q: A steel spoon, a steel tumbler, a key and a chips packet. Which one is not mostly metal?
check.why: A chips packet is shiny, but it is mostly plastic. It is soft and crinkly, and it makes no ting when you tap it. The spoon, the tumbler and the key are metal.

activities.title: The Recycling Corner: sort what we throw away
activities.context: In this activity you set up three bags or boxes at home, for paper, plastic and metal. You sort the clean dry things your family throws away, so they can be made into new things.

materials.item: three old bags or cardboard boxes
paper and crayons, to make a picture label for each bag
clean dry things from the waste: old newspaper, a cardboard box, an empty plastic bottle, a milk packet rinsed and dried, and an empty tin

activities.safety: A grown-up checks that tins have no sharp edges before your child touches them.

schedule.what: Make three picture labels, sort the clean dry waste into the three bags, and keep the corner going all week.

activities.record: Each evening this week, count how many things went into each bag, and make a tally mark on the label.

setup.art: Three bags in a corner of a flat, with picture labels: a newspaper, a plastic bottle and a tin.
setup.caption: 1. Make a picture label for each bag.

setup.art: A boy putting an empty plastic bottle into the plastic bag while a girl holds up a folded newspaper.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each thing into its bag.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a newspaper, a bottle and a tin, one on each label. 2. Stick a label on each bag.
flow.say: We will make a recycling corner. One bag for paper, one for plastic and one for metal. Draw a picture for each bag.
flow.kid: Draw a picture for each bag: paper, plastic and metal.

flow.do: 1. Put the clean dry things in a heap. 2. Your child sorts each one into a bag. 3. Ask how they know.
flow.say: Pick a thing. What is it made of? Which bag does it go in?
flow.kid: Pick a thing. What is it made of? Put it in the right bag.

ask.q: Why does the milk packet go in the plastic bag?
good: It is smooth and bendy, and water does not soak into it.

flow.parent: A kabadiwala or a recycling worker buys paper, plastic and metal separately, because each one is made into new things in a different factory.

flow.do: 1. Put the corner where everyone can reach it. 2. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Why do we keep paper, plastic and metal apart?
flow.kid: Why do we keep them in different bags?

check.q: Why do people sort paper, plastic and metal into different bags?
options: Each one is made into new things in a different way
It makes the bags look nicer
Paper and metal are the same, so it does not matter
check.why: Old paper is soaked and pressed into new paper. Old metal is melted to make new metal. Old plastic is cut and melted too. Each needs its own factory, so they must be sorted first.

games.title: The Sorting Relay: metal basket, not-metal basket
games.players: 2 to 4 people: one calls, and one to three run. With two people, you swap jobs after eight cards.
games.context: This is a running game. The caller reads a thing card. You run and drop the card in the metal basket or the not-metal basket. Then the caller reads the back to check.

items.b: Metal
Not metal. It is mostly wood.
Metal
Not metal. It is cloth.
Metal
Not metal. It is plastic.
Metal
Not metal. It is paper.
Metal
Not metal. It is glass.
Mostly metal, with a plastic handle and a rubber ring. Both baskets are right.
Not metal. It is wood.
Metal. It is a very thin sheet of aluminium.
Not metal. It is mostly plastic, with a very thin shiny coat inside.
Metal

items.f: A chiratta ladle made from a coconut shell
items.b: Not metal. The bowl is coconut shell and the handle is wood.

rules: Put two baskets or buckets at one end of the room. Draw a tick on paper for the metal basket and a cross for the not-metal basket.
Players stand at the other end. Take turns in the same order each time.
The caller reads a thing card out loud and gives it to the next player.
The player runs and drops the card in the metal basket or the not-metal basket, then runs back.
The caller reads the back of the card. A card in the right basket scores one point. For the pressure cooker card, either basket scores.
For a tricky card, like the pressure cooker or the chips packet, a player who says why gets one more point.
After all 16 cards, add up the points. The player with the most points wins. With two people, add up each person's points from both turns.

setup.art: Two buckets at the end of a living room, one with a tick card and one with a cross card, and two children waiting at the other end.
setup.caption: 1. Put a metal basket and a not-metal basket at one end.

setup.art: A girl running across the room with a card that says 'A key', towards the bucket with the tick card.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the card. Run and drop it in a basket.

flow.do: 1. Set out the two baskets with their tick and cross. 2. Clear the floor of anything to trip on.
flow.say: This basket is for metal things. This one is for things that are not metal. I will read a card. You run and drop it in the right basket.
flow.kid: Tick basket is metal. Cross basket is not metal. Listen, then run.

flow.do: 1. Read one card at a time. 2. Your child runs and drops it in. 3. Read the back and give points.
flow.say: A safety pin. Is it metal? Run!
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Is it metal? Run to the right basket.

ask.q: How do you know a safety pin is metal?

flow.parent: The kitchen foil card and the chips packet card are tricky. Both are shiny. Foil is metal, and a chips packet is mostly plastic. If you have real ones, let your child test them: foil stays crumpled when you scrunch it, and a chips packet slowly opens up again. A chips packet is soft and crinkly, and makes no ringing sound when you tap it.

flow.do: Ask the check question at the end of the game.
flow.say: The pressure cooker card could go in both baskets. Why?
flow.kid: Why can the pressure cooker go in both baskets?

check.q: Why can a pressure cooker go in the metal basket and the not-metal basket?
options: It is made of metal and plastic and rubber
It is used in the kitchen
check.why: The pot is metal. The handle is plastic and the ring is rubber. A thing made of more than one material can belong to more than one group.

games.title: Move Like Your Material
games.players: 1 or more players and one caller.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller names a thing. You say what it is made of, and then move like that material: stiff like steel, floppy like cloth, or crumpled like paper.

items.b: Metal. Stand stiff and straight, like a steel rod.
Cloth. Flop and wave your arms softly, like cloth in the wind.
Paper. Crumple down small, like a scrunched-up ball of paper.
Rubber. Stretch your arms wide, then spring back in.
Wood. Lie flat and stiff on the floor, like a plank.
Plastic. Squeeze in a little, then pop back out.
Glass. Stay very, very still and careful, so you don't break.
Dough. Squash down slowly and stay squashed.

rules: The caller reads a thing card out loud.
The players shout what it is made of.
Then the caller reads the move on the back, and everyone moves that way until the caller claps.
After all eight cards, the players make up a move for a new material, like clay or wool.

setup.art: A woman holding a card that says 'A dupatta', and two children waving their arms softly like cloth in the wind.
setup.caption: 1. Hear the thing. Say its material.

setup.art: Two children standing stiff and straight like steel rods, while a woman claps.
setup.caption: 2. Move like the material until the clap.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space. 2. Show one card and act out its move yourself.
flow.say: I will name a thing. You tell me what it is made of. Then we move like that material. Watch me be a steel spoon.
flow.kid: Listen to the thing. Say what it is made of. Then move like it.

flow.do: 1. Read each card. 2. Your child names the material. 3. Read the move and clap to stop.
flow.say: A dupatta! What is it made of? Yes, cloth. Now flop like cloth.
flow.kid: What is it made of? Now move like that material.

ask.q: Why do we move stiffly for steel and softly for cloth?

flow.parent: This game is about properties, which means what a material is like. Name them as you play: hard, soft, stiff, floppy, stretchy.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which material would you move like if I said 'a steel katori'?
flow.kid: How would you move for a steel katori?

check.q: A steel katori is made of the same material as which of these?
check.why: A katori and a spoon are both steel, a metal. They have different shapes, but the same material.

projects.title: My Sorting Book
projects.context: In this project you make a small book of sorts. Each day you sort a different heap at home and draw your groups on one page.

materials.item: three sheets of paper, folded in half and stapled or tied with string into a little book
crayons or sketch pens

schedule.what: Sort the steel vessels and other things in one kitchen drawer or shelf by material. Draw the groups on page 1.
Sort your toys with a question you choose. Draw the groups on page 2 and write the question.
Sort the clean washing by a new question, such as 'Is it cotton?' or 'Whose is it?' Draw the groups on page 3, then show the book to the family.

projects.record: The finished three-page book. Each page shows the groups and the question that made them.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper folded in half and stapled into a small book, with 'My Sorting Book' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Make a little book from three folded sheets.

setup.art: A book page with two circles: one with drawings of toy cars and blocks, the other with a doll and a cloth rabbit, and a question written at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, sort a heap and draw the groups.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up helps make the book. 2. Your child sorts one kitchen shelf by material. 3. They draw each group on page 1.
flow.say: Today we sort a kitchen shelf by what things are made of. Then draw your groups.
flow.kid: Sort the shelf by material. Draw each group on page 1.

flow.do: 1. Your child picks a question for the toys. 2. They sort the toys and draw the groups on page 2.
flow.say: Today you choose the question. How will you sort your toys?
flow.kid: Choose a question. Sort your toys. Draw the groups.

flow.do: 1. Sort the clean washing with a new question. 2. Draw page 3. 3. Your child shows the book and reads each question.
flow.say: Today we sort the washing. Then show your book to everyone.
flow.kid: Sort the washing. Draw page 3. Show your book.

check.q: You sort your toys by the question 'Is it soft?' Where does a cloth rabbit go?
check.why: A cloth rabbit is soft, so it answers yes to the question 'Is it soft?'. It goes in the soft group.

challenges.title: A Raft for a Small Toy
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. You use what you found in the Sink or Float Sort to build a raft that carries a small toy on a bucket of water.
challenges.problem: A small toy needs to cross a bucket of water without getting wet. Can you build a raft from things that float?
constraints: The raft must float with the toy on it for a count of twenty.
materials: an empty plastic bottle with its cap on
a small plastic toy or an eraser
a bucket half full of water
general: Tape ice-cream sticks side by side into a flat raft.
Tape plastic bottle caps under the corners, so the raft sits higher.
In many parts of India, such as Assam, people tie bamboo poles together to make rafts.
creative: Lay an empty plastic bottle on its side, and tape the sticks on top of it.
Use a steel katori as a boat. It floated in the Sink or Float Sort.
Make the raft wider, so it does not tip over.
challenges.your_turn: Build your raft and test it with the toy. If it tips or sinks, change one thing and try again. Draw your best raft, and colour each material in a different colour.

setup.art: Ice-cream sticks taped side by side into a small square raft, with bottle caps taped under the corners.
setup.caption: 1. Build a raft from things that floated.

setup.art: A small toy elephant sitting on the raft, floating in a bucket of water, while a girl counts on her fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Put the toy on and count to twenty.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem to your child. 2. Look back at the float pile from the Sink or Float Sort.
flow.say: The toy wants to cross the water and stay dry. Which things floated in the Sink or Float Sort? Which would make a good raft?
flow.kid: Which things floated in the Sink or Float Sort? Which could make a raft?

ask.q: Which things will you use? Why?
good: Not the coin, because it sank.

flow.do: 1. Your child chooses floaters and lays them out. 2. Help tape them together.
flow.say: Lay out your raft. I will hold the sticks while you tape them.
flow.kid: Put your floaters together. Tape them into a raft.

flow.do: 1. Put the raft on the water. 2. Your child puts the toy in the middle. 3. Count to twenty.
flow.say: Put your toy on the raft, right in the middle. Let's count to twenty. Is the toy dry?
flow.kid: Put the toy on. Count to twenty. Is it dry?

good: Put the toy in the middle.

flow.parent: If the raft tips, the toy may be too far to one side, or the raft too narrow. A small toy or an eraser needs about ten sticks. If the raft sinks low, add more sticks, or tape the sticks onto an empty plastic bottle. Change one thing and test again.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Why should we not use coins to build a raft?
flow.kid: Why not build a raft from coins?

check.q: Why are ice-cream sticks better than coins for a raft?
options: Wood floated in the Sink or Float Sort, and the coin sank
The sticks are a nicer colour
check.why: In the Sink or Float Sort, wood floated and the coin sank. A raft needs things that float, so the test tells us what to choose.

items.p: Ask 'Is it metal?' about each thing. Colour the metal things grey. Leave the others white.
items.why: A key, a tumbler and a coin are metal. They are hard and shiny, and they ring when tapped. A pencil is wood, a towel is cloth and a comb is plastic.
items.art: Six small pictures in a row: a key, a pencil, a steel tumbler, a folded towel, a coin and a comb.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to its material.
pairs: A spoon that rings when tapped
items.why: Most rolling pins are wood, windows are glass and buckets are plastic. A newspaper is paper. A spoon that rings is metal.
items.art: Five things on the left (a rolling pin, a window, a bucket, a newspaper, a spoon) and five material words on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Three of these are made of plastic. Which one is not?
items.why: A bottle cap, a comb and a bucket are usually plastic. A steel spoon is metal. It is shiny and cold, and it rings when tapped.

items.p: A key, a coin and a spoon are put together in one group. What question was asked?
items.why: A key, a coin and a spoon are all metal. None of them is soft or see-through.

items.p: Which of these is a good question for sorting a heap of things into two groups?
items.why: A good sorting question has a clear answer, yes or no, for every thing. 'Is it nice?' is different for each person.

items.p: All metal things sink in water.
items.why: False. In the Sink or Float Sort, the steel katori floated. Big steel ships float too, because their shape holds air.

items.p: Draw a bucket of water. Draw the steel spoon where it ended up, and the steel katori where it ended up.
items.a: The spoon at the bottom of the bucket, and the katori floating on top.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the spoon at the bottom and the katori on top, even though both are steel.
items.art: An empty outline of a bucket with a wavy line for the water.

items.p: A steel katori floats right way up. What happens if you pour water into it, and why? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: It sinks. The water pushes the air out of the katori, and without the air the water cannot hold it up.
items.why: A strong answer says what happened (it sank) and why (the air inside was gone).

items.p: Priya and her brother Farhan are sorting a knife with a steel blade and a plastic handle.

views.says: It goes with the metal things. The blade is the important part.
It goes in both groups, because it is made of metal and plastic.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right. Say it, and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For Priya: the knife really is made of two materials. For Farhan: the blade is the part that does the cutting, so it is fair to group it with metal things.
items.why: Both are partly right. A thing made of two materials can go in two groups. Which group you choose depends on why you are sorting.

items.p: Draw something at home that is made of two materials. Colour each material a different colour.
items.a: For example, a pressure cooker with a metal pot and a black plastic handle, in two colours.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two clear parts, each a different material, and the child can name both.

items.p: You have a clear bottle. You do not know if it is glass or plastic. What is a good test?
opts: Tap it with a spoon and listen
items.why: Glass goes ting and plastic goes tock. Lifting it helps too: glass is heavier. The colour does not tell you.

items.p: Sort these by the question 'Will it float in water?'
items: A steel katori, right way up
items.why: Wood floated. The solid metal things sank. The katori floated because its shape held air.

items.p: Some people say, 'Heavy things sink and light things float.' A big wooden log is very heavy. What does it do in a river? What would you tell them? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The log floats. So heavy things do not always sink. A small key is light, and it sinks. What a thing is made of, and its shape, matter more than how heavy it is.
items.why: A strong answer uses an example that does not fit the rule, like a heavy log that floats or a light key that sinks.

items.p: In the Sink or Float Sort, the metal group had a spoon, a coin, a key and a katori. Only the katori floated. How many metal things sank?
items.why: 4 metal things, and 1 floated. 4 take away 1 is 3. The spoon, the coin and the key sank.

items.p: Here is a pencil. Say what each part is made of, and a grown-up writes the word.
labels: the long outside, under the paint
the shiny band holding the pink end
items.why: A pencil is wood outside with a grey graphite stick inside. Many pencils have a rubber at the end, held on by a thin metal band. So a pencil belongs to several material groups.
items.art: A pencil with a pink rubber and a shiny band, with four empty labels pointing to its parts.

items.p: Rukmini, aged 7, and her cousin Kavya, aged 6, are sorting the steel katori after the Sink or Float Sort.

views.says: The katori goes in the metal group. It is made of steel.
The katori goes in the float group. I saw it float.

items.ask: Who is right? Can they both be right? Say why. A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: A strong answer says both are right, because they asked different questions. Rukmini asked 'What is it made of?' Kavya asked 'Does it float?' The katori is metal and it floats, right way up.
items.why: The same thing can be in different groups when you ask different questions. The groups come from the question.

items.p: Draw a new thing made of steel that you think would float. Show the air inside it.
items.a: For example, a steel tiffin box with its lid shut, a steel plate, or a steel boat, with the air coloured in.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a hollow or wide steel shape that holds air, like the katori.

items.p: One child sorted some toys into 'red' and 'not red'. Another child sorted the same toys into 'plastic' and 'not plastic'. Can both ways be right? Say why. A grown-up can write your answer.
items.a: Yes. Each question makes its own groups. One child sorted by colour and the other sorted by material. Both are good ways to sort.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same heap can be sorted in many ways, and each question gives different groups.

items.p: All plastic things float in water.
items.why: False. A bottle cap floats, but many plastic combs sink. There are many kinds of plastic, and they do not all do the same thing.

items.p: Sort these by the question 'Can you see through it?'
items.why: Glass and clear plastic let light through, so you can see through them. Wood, steel and paper do not.
items.art: Six small pictures in a row: a window, a rolling pin, a clear bottle, a steel tumbler, a glass jar and a paper bag.

quiz.p: What does it mean to sort things?
opts: To put alike things together in groups
quiz.why: Sorting means putting things that are alike in one way into the same group.

quiz.p: You ask 'Is it metal?' about each thing. Which one goes in the yes group?
quiz.why: A steel tumbler is metal. A towel is cloth and a paper bag is paper, so they go in the no group.

quiz.p: A rolling pin has thin brown lines on it, called grain. What is it made of?
quiz.why: A wooden rolling pin is made of wood. You can see thin lines, called grain, on it.

quiz.p: Which of these is made of glass?
opts: A bangle you can see through that goes ting
quiz.why: A see-through bangle that rings when tapped is glass. A chappal is rubber and a pencil is mostly wood.

quiz.p: A clear bottle could be glass or plastic. What should you do to find out?
opts: Look at the label on the shelf
quiz.why: A test tells you. Glass goes ting and is heavy. Plastic goes tock and is light.

quiz.p: A steel tumbler and a plastic tumbler are the same size. You hold one in each hand. Which feels colder?
quiz.why: Steel takes warmth from your hand quickly, so it feels cold. Plastic does not, so it feels warmer. This is one test for telling materials apart.

quiz.p: A steel spoon sinks in water. What will a steel katori do, put in the water right way up?
quiz.why: The katori floats, because its bowl shape holds air. Both are steel, but their shapes make them do different things.

quiz.p: Big ships are made of steel. Why do they float?
opts: Their shape holds a lot of air inside
The sea is too deep for them to sink
quiz.why: A ship is a huge hollow shape, like a giant katori. The air inside helps the water hold it up.

quiz.p: Before testing, you guess that the pencil will float. What should you do next?
opts: Test it in the water and see
Say you were right without testing
quiz.why: A guess is where science starts. Then you test it, and the test shows if the guess was right.

quiz.p: You guessed that all the metal things would sink. The katori floated. What does that tell you?
opts: Your guess was wrong for the katori, so you learned something new
The katori is not really metal
quiz.why: The katori is metal, and it floated. When a test does not match a guess, you learn something new.

videos.title: A huge cruise ship floats out of its shipyard
videos.why: Shows a huge steel ship being floated out of its dock into the water, like a giant version of the katori in the Sink or Float Sort.
videos.check: Found by search: "Big Ship Launch: Float Out of Cruise Ship DISNEY WISH at Meyer Werft Shipyard" by HD1080ide, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Plastic pieces sorted in a sink and float tank
videos.why: Shows a recycling line where shredded plastic is washed and separated in water tanks: some pieces sink and some float. It is the same test as the Sink or Float Sort.
videos.check: Found by search: "Most Efficient Plastic Recycling Washing & Sink Float System" by Paul Vanderpool, 2 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: A kabadiwala sorting scrap into paper, plastic and metal
videos.why: Shows how sorting by material lets old things be sold and made into new things, as in the Recycling Corner.
videos.check: Find a real documentary or news clip from an Indian city. Check that it does not show child workers.

applications: Kabadiwalas and recycling workers sort paper, plastic, glass and metal, so each can be made into new things.
Recycling plants float shredded plastic in water. Pieces of water bottles sink, and pieces of bottle caps float, so the two kinds of plastic come apart.
Farmers soak seeds in water before sowing. Seeds that float are often empty or damaged, so the farmer keeps the ones that sink.
Shipbuilders, such as those at Cochin Shipyard in Kochi, shape steel into hollow hulls so that ships float.
Shops sort what they sell, so people can find things fast: steel vessels on one shelf, glass on another.

spotted.text: A vessel shop in Thrissur, with steel tumblers, brass lamps and aluminium pots each on their own shelf.
spotted.art: A small shop with shelves of shining steel tumblers, brass lamps and aluminium pots, each kind on its own shelf.

spotted.text: Dabbawalas in Mumbai sorting hundreds of tiffin boxes by the coloured marks painted on their lids.
spotted.art: Men and women in white caps at a railway station, sorting rows of tiffin boxes with coloured marks on the lids.

spotted.text: Bangle shops in Laad Bazaar, Hyderabad, with bangles sorted into shining rows by colour and size.
spotted.art: A shop wall covered in rows of bangles, each row a different colour.

spotted.text: Steel ferry boats crossing the water in Kochi, full of people, floating like big katoris.
spotted.art: A steel ferry boat full of people crossing calm water, with green trees on the far shore.

spotted.text: A kabadiwala in Kolkata with neat piles of newspaper, plastic bottles and metal tins on a hand cart.
spotted.art: A woman beside a hand cart with three neat piles: newspapers tied with string, plastic bottles and metal tins.

open_questions.q: How do babies begin to sort the world into groups before they can talk?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that babies only a few months old notice groups, such as pictures of cats and pictures of dogs. Nobody knows exactly how they do it.

open_questions.q: Can machines ever sort every kind of plastic so all of it can be made into new things?
open_questions.why_open: Many plastics look alike. Recycling plants use water tanks, air and light to sort them, but much plastic still cannot be sorted well.

open_questions.q: Could people make a material as light as air and as strong as steel?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made solids that are almost all air, like aerogel, but they are not as strong as steel. Many are still trying.

ask_kids: What question could we ask to sort the vegetables in the fridge?
Can you find three things on the way to the shop made of the same material?
Which things in the bathroom do you think would float? Why?
Is there anything in this room that is made of two materials?
How would you sort your clothes, if you could choose any question?
Why do you think a boat floats, even when it is full of people?

jokes.j: Why did the spoon go to the bottom of the bucket?
jokes.a: It was feeling a bit low!

jokes.j: What did the katori say to the water?
jokes.a: Hold me up, I'm full of air!

jokes.j: What do you call a wooden spoon that cannot sink?
What kind of music do steel spoons like?
Why did the sock go in the cloth pile?
What has teeth but never bites?
Why do cooks love steel spoons?
jokes.a: They are great at stirring things up!

maths.problem: In the Sink or Float Sort, 8 things go into the water. 5 float. How many sink?
maths.explain: Count 8 fingers. Fold down 5 for the things that floated. 3 fingers are left, so 3 things sank. 8 take away 5 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the Sink or Float Sort, where you put eight things into a bucket of water one at a time.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how many are in the second group when we know the total and the first group.

maths.problem: In the Yes-or-No Sort, the metal circle has 4 things and the not-metal circle has 6 things. Then a knife is laid across the edge of both circles, so it counts in both. How many things are in each circle now?
maths.answer: 5 things in the metal circle and 7 things in the not-metal circle.
maths.explain: The knife is metal and plastic, so it counts in both circles. 4 and 1 more is 5. 6 and 1 more is 7.
maths.context: This is about the Yes-or-No Sort, where the knife went across the edge of both circles.
maths.why_maths: Counting a thing that belongs to two groups shows how groups can overlap.

maths.problem: Here are the tally marks from a Recycling Corner for one week: paper 6, plastic 9, metal 2. Which bag filled up fastest? What might the family do to throw away less of it?
maths.answer: Plastic, with 9 things. They could carry a cloth bag to the shop, or buy things with less plastic wrapping.
maths.explain: 9 is more than 6, and 6 is more than 2. So the plastic bag got the most things. The numbers show where most of the waste comes from.
maths.context: This is about the Recycling Corner, where you made a tally mark for each thing you sorted.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks turn a week of sorting into numbers we can compare and use to decide what to change.

warmup.q: What question would put a key and a coin in the same group?
Did the steel katori float or sink, right way up?
Why did the katori sink when it was full of water?
warmup.a: The water pushed out the air that helped hold it up.

warmup.q: Does a pencil float or sink?
warmup.a: It floats, because it is mostly wood.

warmup.q: A knife has a steel blade and a plastic handle. How many materials is that?
In the story, what was the bowl of Ammamma's chiratta ladle made from?
warmup.a: Half a coconut shell. The handle was wood.

founder: ideas/by_topic/materials-and-their-properties.md: the notebook's 'dance' and 'physical games' ideas (moving like a material, guessing a material) shaped Move Like Your Material and the Sorting Relay. Its sound, light and heat activities belong to other units.

The Class 3 unit on this subtopic uses one heap sorted by three rules, a scratch ladder, branching keys, sorting by sound, the Floor Venn, dal cleaning, a model recycling line, star sorting and oobleck. So this unit uses a yes-or-no sort, odd one out plates, a home recycling corner and a sink or float sort instead, and leaves Venn diagrams and keys for Class 3.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, Unit 4.3 'Sorting materials': sorting with a question such as 'Is it metal?', sorting by feel, inventing tests, and recycling.
science: Archimedes, On Floating Bodies (3rd century BCE): a body in water is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it pushes aside.
A. L. Lavoisier, Traité élémentaire de chimie (1789), with 13 plates drawn by Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier. Its table of simple substances lists 33, including light and caloric.
H. Cavendish, 'Experiments on Air', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 74 (1784): water formed by burning inflammable air (hydrogen) with air.

Plastic resin identification codes 1 to 7. Polypropylene and polyethylene (often used for bottle caps) are less dense than water and float. PET (used for water bottles) is denser and sinks, which recycling plants use in sink-float tanks.
P. C. Quinn, P. D. Eimas and S. L. Rosenkrantz, 'Evidence for representations of perceptually similar natural categories by 3-month-old and 4-month-old infants', Perception 22 (1993).
Silica aerogel is mostly air, often more than 99% by volume, and is among the lightest solids made.

playtest: Walked through the unit as a parent and child in a flat. Sink or Float Sort: the minutes add up to 20, the metal group is four, wood two and plastic two, and the thin katori floats while the comb may do either, which the step says. Yes-or-No Sort counts match the maths question. Fixed the Sorting Relay so it plays with 2 to 4 people and has no solo rule, replaced a vague sound line, a repeated knife quiz question (now a feel-cold test), a repeated lungs example and a weak joke, and made the milk packet answer and a true or false answer consistent.
